items.prose: A two-digit number's complement to 100 has its tens digit up to 9 and its units digit up to 10. Show why. Take a number $10t + u$ whose units digit $u$ is not 0.
items.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Units: $u$ needs $10 - u$ more to make one whole ten.
That new ten joins the $t$ tens, so we now have $t + 1$ tens.
100 is 10 tens, so we still need $10 - (t + 1) = 9 - t$ tens.
So the complement is $9 - t$ tens and $10 - u$ units.

explain.text: Filling the units makes one more ten, so $t + 1$ tens are in hand. Ten tens make 100, so $9 - t$ more are needed. For 37: $10 - 7 = 3$ units and $9 - 3 = 6$ tens give 63.

items.title: Checking a day's trading
items.prompt:
You bought one share at £47.96 and another at £48.04. Later you sold both at £51.25 each. At the moment you sold, the bid was £51.25 and the ask was £51.42.

(a) Find the total cost of the two buys. Name the mental method you used.

(b) Find the profit on each share, and the total profit.

(c) Find the spread when you sold, by counting up. What would it cost to buy both shares back at the ask?

(d) A colleague says your total profit was £16.50. Use a rounded estimate to show whether that can be right.
items.model:
**(a)** Pair the pence: 96p and 4p make £1. So the cost is £47 + £48 + £1 = £96.00. (Adding from the left also works: £47.96 + £48 = £95.96, then 4p more is £96.00.)

**(b)** Share 1: £51.25 − £48 = £3.25, and £48 was 4p more than £47.96, so give 4p back: **£3.29**. Share 2: £51.25 − £48 = £3.25, and £48 was 4p less than £48.04, so take 4p more off: **£3.21**. Total: £3.29 + £3.21 = **£6.50**. Check: the sales bring in 2 × £51.25 = £102.50, and £102.50 − £96.00 = £6.50.

**(c)** Count up from the bid: £51.25 to £51.30 is 5p, and £51.30 to £51.42 is 12p. The spread is **17p**. Buying both back at the ask costs £51.42 + £51.42 = **£102.84**: £102 from the pounds, then 42p + 42p = 84p.

**(d)** Round every price to the nearest pound: the buys are about £48 + £48 = £96 and the sales about £51 + £51 = £102. The profit is about £6. Rounding moved each price by at most 25p, so four prices move the estimate by at most £1. £16.50 is more than £10 away from £6, so it cannot be right. It looks like an extra ten crept in. The true profit is £6.50.

rubric.text: Finds £96.00 for the two buys. Names a mental method, such as pairing 96p with 4p or adding from the left.
Finds £3.29 profit on the first share, correcting £3.25 in the right direction.
Finds £3.21 profit on the second share, correcting £3.25 in the right direction.
Finds the 17p spread by counting up from the bid to the ask, showing the steps.
Finds £102.84 as the cost of buying both back at the ask.
Estimates the profit at about £6 from rounded prices and explains why £16.50 is too far away to be right.
